claim: GM neurons exhibit animal-to-animal variability in cable lengths with a coefficient of variation of 0.4.
source: We quantify animal-to-animal variability in cable lengths (CV = 0.4) and branching patterns in the Gastric Mill (GM) neuron, an identified neuron type with highly-conserved physiological properties in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of Cancer borealis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by morphological measurements presented in Figure 2C showing total cable lengths across 14 GM neurons.

claim: GM neurons exhibit animal-to-animal variability in branching patterns.
source: We quantify animal-to-animal variability in cable lengths (CV = 0.4) and branching patterns in the Gastric Mill (GM) neuron, an identified neuron type with highly-conserved physiological properties in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of Cancer borealis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2D showing variable branch point numbers and Figure 3 showing variable axonal branching patterns.

claim: GM neurons have highly-conserved physiological properties.
source: We quantify animal-to-animal variability in cable lengths (CV = 0.4) and branching patterns in the Gastric Mill (GM) neuron, an identified neuron type with highly-conserved physiological properties in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of Cancer borealis.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by references to previous work showing conserved physiological waveforms in STG neurons.

claim: Apparent reversal potentials of inhibitory responses in GM neurons are relatively invariant across sites with a mean coefficient of variation of 0.04 ± 0.01.
source: Apparent Erevs were relatively invariant across sites (mean CV ± SD = 0.04 ± 0.01; 7–20 sites in each of 10 neurons), which ranged between 100–800 µm from the somatic recording site.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 8 and 9 showing reversal potential measurements across multiple sites in 10 neurons.

claim: GM neurons are electrotonically compact with an estimated electrotonic length constant greater than 1.5 mm.
source: Thus, GM neurons are remarkably electrotonically compact (estimated λ > 1.5 mm).
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by reversal potential measurements showing minimal hyperpolarizing shift across distances of 100-800 µm, which is compared to simulations in Figure 7.

claim: Electrotonically compact structures in consort with graded transmission provide a solution to observed morphological variability in the STG.
source: Electrotonically compact structures, in consort with graded transmission, provide an elegant solution to observed morphological variability in the STG.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and is discussed in detail in the Discussion section.

claim: Neuronal circuits can generate stable output despite variable underlying parameters across animals.
source: Neuronal circuits can generate stable output despite variable underlying parameters across animals (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Marder, 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Circuit function can be maintained across animals despite variable synaptic, intrinsic, and modulator-induced currents in identified constituent neurons.
source: Work in invertebrate central pattern-generating circuits shows that circuit function can be maintained across animals despite variable synaptic, intrinsic, and modulator-induced currents in identified constituent neurons (Prinz et al., 2004; Schulz et al., 2006; Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Goaillard et al., 2009; Norris et al., 2011; Marder, 2011; Roffman et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2013; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Rodriguez et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Neurons compensate for variable ionic conductances at the circuit and single-neuron levels.
source: This previous work has revealed the principle that neurons compensate for variable ionic conductances at the circuit (Grashow et al., 2010) and single-neuron levels (Tobin et al., 2009; Ball et al., 2010; O'Leary et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The unique physiology of any given neuron is a consequence of its palette of ionic conductances and its morphology.
source: The unique physiology of any given neuron is a consequence of its palette of ionic conductances, and its morphology (Mainen and Sejnowski, 1996; Vetter et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A neuron's distributed geometric cable properties shape passive current flow and voltage propagation.
source: A neuron's distributed, geometric cable properties: the length, diameter, taper, and branching of its neurites, shape passive current flow and voltage propagation (Rall, 1959, 1977; Goldstein and Rall, 1974).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to foundational work on cable theory.

claim: Electrotonic structure plays a central role in determining whether voltage signals arising at disparate sites across the dendritic tree are integrated or segregated.
source: This resulting electrotonic structure plays a central role in determining whether voltage signals arising at disparate sites across the dendritic tree are integrated or segregated (Rall, 1959, 1967, 1969a, 1969b; Rall and Rinzel, 1973, 1974; Goldstein and Rall, 1974; Agmon-Snir and Segev, 1993;﻿ Vetter et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Ion channel expression, when superimposed on morphology, gives rise to neuronal physiology, input-output computations, and circuit-level function.
source: In this way, ion channel expression, when superimposed on morphology, gives rise to neuronal physiology, input-output computations, and circuit-level function (for reviews, see Koch and Segev, 2000; London and Häusser, 2005).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The STG is a central pattern-generating circuit composed of 26–27 neurons.
source: In the present study, we investigated the physiological consequences of animal-to-animal variability in neuronal morphology in the crab stomatogastric ganglion (STG), a central pattern-generating circuit composed of 26–27 neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and is established knowledge about the STG.

claim: The identified neuron types of the STG exhibit highly conserved physiological waveforms and circuit-level functions.
source: The identified neuron types of the STG exhibit highly conserved physiological waveforms and circuit-level functions (Harris-Warrick et al., 1992), despite their complex and variable morphologies across animals (Wilensky et al., 2003; Baldwin and Graubard, 1995; Bucher et al., 2007; Goeritz et al., 2013; Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: STG neurons display complex and variable morphologies across animals.
source: The identified neuron types of the STG exhibit highly conserved physiological waveforms and circuit-level functions (Harris-Warrick et al., 1992), despite their complex and variable morphologies across animals (Wilensky et al., 2003; Baldwin and Graubard, 1995; Bucher et al., 2007; Goeritz et al., 2013; Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: STG neurons display large somata (50–100 µm in diameter).
source: STG neurons display large somata (50–100 µm in diameter) and primary neurites that ramify throughout the STG neuropil (Selverston et al., 1976; King, 1976a, 1976b; Baldwin and Graubard, 1995; Kilman and Marder, 1996).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: STG neurons have primary neurites that ramify throughout the STG neuropil.
source: STG neurons display large somata (50–100 µm in diameter) and primary neurites that ramify throughout the STG neuropil (Selverston et al., 1976; King, 1976a, 1976b; Baldwin and Graubard, 1995; Kilman and Marder, 1996).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptic transmission between STG neurons is predominantly graded, inhibitory cholinergic and glutamatergic transmission.
source: Synaptic transmission between neurons is predominantly graded, inhibitory cholinergic and glutamatergic transmission (Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Maynard and Walton, 1975; Graubard et al., 1980; Manor et al., 1997, 1999).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptic sites in STG neurons are sparsely distributed throughout finer processes in the neuropil region.
source: Synaptic sites are sparsely distributed throughout finer processes in the neuropil region (King, 1976a, 1976b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There are no synapses on somata in STG neurons.
source: There are no synapses on somata in these neurons (King, 1976a, 1976b) and spike initiation zones are located in the periphery where axons exit the ganglion (Raper, 1979; Miller, 1980).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spike initiation zones in STG neurons are located in the periphery where axons exit the ganglion.
source: There are no synapses on somata in these neurons (King, 1976a, 1976b) and spike initiation zones are located in the periphery where axons exit the ganglion (Raper, 1979; Miller, 1980).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptic integration and release in STG neurons occurs predominantly in the neuropil.
source: Thus, synaptic integration and release occurs predominantly in the neuropil.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and is inferred from the location of synaptic sites and spike initiation zones.

claim: In individual STG neurons, pre- and post-synaptic sites are often tightly apposed on the same neurites.
source: In individual STG neurons, pre- and post-synaptic sites are often tightly apposed on the same neurites (King, 1976a, 1976b).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The juxtaposition of synaptic input and output in STG neurons suggests that current will flow in all directions across the neurite tree.
source: This juxtaposition of synaptic input and output suggests that current will flow in all directions across the neurite tree, centripetally and centrifugally, in the intact circuit, and allow for integration of voltage signals arising from disparate loci on the neurite tree, should the neuron be sufficiently electrotonically compact.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and is inferred from the anatomical arrangement of synaptic sites.

claim: Previous investigation of electrotonic structure in STG neurons employed simultaneous electrophysiological recordings at the soma and primary neurite with electrodes separated by several hundred microns.
source: Previous investigation of electrotonic structure in STG neurons employed simultaneous electrophysiological recordings at the soma and primary neurite, wherein electrodes were separated by several hundred microns (Miller, 1980; Golowasch and Marder, 1992).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous recordings in STG neurons showed low-pass filtering of high-frequency voltage events across the primary neurite.
source: These recordings showed low-pass filtering of high-frequency voltage events across the primary neurite, as is typically imposed by the membrane capacitance (Rall, 1977).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Slow voltage oscillations in STG neurons were subject to less electrotonic decrement than high-frequency events.
source: In contrast, slow voltage oscillations were subject to less electrotonic decrement.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and is based on previous experimental findings.

claim: The frequency-dependent decay of electrical signals in STG neurons was consistent with contemporary theoretical and experimental works.
source: This frequency-dependent decay of electrical signals was consistent with the findings of contemporary theoretical and experimental works (Rall, 1977; Johnston and Brown, 1983; Spruston et al., 1993, 1994; Jaffe and Carnevale, 1999).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: STG circuit function is mediated predominantly by graded transmission.
source: This early characterization of electrotonic structure in the STG may have been a satisfactory description at the time, given that STG circuit function is mediated predominantly by graded transmission (Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Maynard and Walton, 1975; Graubard et al., 1980; Manor et al., 1997, 1999) and slow oscillations (Graubard and Ross, 1985; Ross and Graubard, 1989), and continues to oscillate in the absence of spikes (Graubard, 1978; Raper, 1979; Graubard et al., 1983;Anderson and Barker, 1981).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: STG circuit function is mediated predominantly by slow oscillations.
source: This early characterization of electrotonic structure in the STG may have been a satisfactory description at the time, given that STG circuit function is mediated predominantly by graded transmission (Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Maynard and Walton, 1975; Graubard et al., 1980; Manor et al., 1997, 1999) and slow oscillations (Graubard and Ross, 1985; Ross and Graubard, 1989), and continues to oscillate in the absence of spikes (Graubard, 1978; Raper, 1979; Graubard et al., 1983;Anderson and Barker, 1981).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The STG continues to oscillate in the absence of spikes.
source: This early characterization of electrotonic structure in the STG may have been a satisfactory description at the time, given that STG circuit function is mediated predominantly by graded transmission (Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Maynard and Walton, 1975; Graubard et al., 1980; Manor et al., 1997, 1999) and slow oscillations (Graubard and Ross, 1985; Ross and Graubard, 1989), and continues to oscillate in the absence of spikes (Graubard, 1978; Raper, 1979; Graubard et al., 1983;Anderson and Barker, 1981).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pre- and post-synaptic connections in STG neurons are located at more distal, finer processes.
source: Relevant voltage events must arise at more distal, finer processes, where pre- and post-synaptic connections are located (King, 1976a, 1976b; Kilman and Marder, 1996).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A full experimental characterization of the electrotonic structure of STG neurons requires electrophysiologically sampling numerous sites across the dendritic tree.
source: Thus, a full experimental characterization of the electrotonic structure of STG neurons requires electrophysiologically sampling numerous sites across the dendritic tree.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Introduction and is inferred from the limitations of previous work.

claim: The GM neuron is one of fourteen identified neuron types in the STG.
source: The gastric mill (GM) neuron is one of fourteen identified neuron types in the STG.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is established knowledge about the STG.

claim: There are typically four GM neurons in each animal.
source: There are typically four GM neurons in each animal.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is established knowledge about the STG.

claim: GM neurons project axons to and innervate extrinsic gastric muscles 1a, 1b, 2, 3a, and 3b via the anterior lateral and dorsal ventral nerves.
source: The GM neuron ramifies throughout the neuropil region and can be distinguished by multiple axons, projecting to and innervating extrinsic gastric muscles 1a, 1b, 2, 3a, and 3b via the anterior lateral (aln) and dorsal ventral (dvn) nerves (Maynard and Dando, 1974; Selverston and Mulloney, 1974; Weimann et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GM neurons participate in the episodic gastric mill rhythm.
source: GM neurons participate in the episodic gastric mill rhythm (Hartline and Maynard, 1975).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GM activity evokes rhythmic contractions of its target muscles, resulting in grinding movements of the gastric mill ossicles and attached teeth for internal chewing of food.
source: When bursting (Figure 1C), GM activity evokes rhythmic contractions of its target muscles, resulting in grinding movements of the gastric mill ossicles and attached teeth for internal chewing of food (Russell, 1985; Heinzel, 1988).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GM neurons are unambiguously identified by matching their spiking activity with spiking units on extracellular nerves known to contain GM axonal projections.
source: GM neurons are unambiguously identified by matching their spiking activity with spiking units on extracellular nerves known to contain GM axonal projections (Figure 1D; Maynard and Dando, 1974).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: GM neurons exhibit large somata with a mean diameter of 74 ± 13 µm.
source: GM neurons exhibit large somata (with a mean diameter ± SD of 74 ± 13 µm) and expansive neurite branches that span the neuropil region.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on measurements from confocal image stacks.

claim: Non-axonal neurite branches of GM neurons spanned an average ellipsoid volume of 4.98 ± 1.43 × 10^6 µm^3.
source: Non-axonal neurite branches spanned an average ellipsoid volume of 4.98 ± 1.43 × 106 µm3 (mean ± SD).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on measurements from confocal image stacks.

claim: GM neurons have a mean total cable length of 8840 ± 3678 µm.
source: These neurons present expansive structures, with a mean total cable length of 8840 ± 3678 µm (Figure 2C) and numerous branch points (mean number of branch points ± SD was 155 ± 126; Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on skeletal reconstructions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GM neurons have a mean number of branch points of 155 ± 126.
source: These neurons present expansive structures, with a mean total cable length of 8840 ± 3678 µm (Figure 2C) and numerous branch points (mean number of branch points ± SD was 155 ± 126; Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on skeletal reconstructions shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Total cable lengths and branch point numbers in GM neurons varied by 40% of the mean (CV = 0.4 for both metrics).
source: Notably, across animals, total cable lengths and branch point numbers varied by 40% of the mean (CV = 0.4 for both metrics).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on measurements from skeletal reconstructions.

claim: The mean soma-to-tip path length in GM neurons was 450 ± 80 µm.
source: The mean soma-to-tip path length was 450 ± 80 µm.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on measurements from skeletal reconstructions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GM neurons display tortuous three-dimensional structures.
source: In Figure 2A and B, it is visually evident that GM neurons display tortuous three-dimensional structures.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on visual inspection of confocal images and skeletal reconstructions in Figure 2.

claim: The mean tortuosity across all GM neurons is 2.1 ± 0.5.
source: Across GM neurons, tortuosity distributions vary. But, each neuron presents a broad tortuosity distribution and has a mean tortuosity that is modestly greater than one (Figure 2E; the mean across all neurons is 2.1 ± 0.5).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on measurements from skeletal reconstructions shown in Figure 2F.

claim: GM neurons are tortuous and expansive, and somewhat variable in their macroscopic morphology.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that GM neurons are tortuous and expansive, and somewhat variable in their macroscopic morphology.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is a summary of the morphological data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Pre- and post-synaptic connections in STG neurons are distributed throughout the finer process within the STG neuropil.
source: Previous work suggests that pre- and post-synaptic connections are distributed throughout the finer process within the STG neuropil (King, 1976b; Kilman and Marder, 1996) and that spike initiation zones are located in the periphery, where the axons exit the neuropil (Raper, 1979; Miller, 1980).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GM neurons typically have between 3–5 axons.
source: GM neurons typically have between 3–5 axons (Figure 3A), with at least one projection to the aln and one projection to the dvn (this is consistent with previous findings; Maynard and Dando, 1974).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on data shown in Figure 3A and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GM neurons have at least one axonal projection to the aln and one projection to the dvn.
source: GM neurons typically have between 3–5 axons (Figure 3A), with at least one projection to the aln and one projection to the dvn (this is consistent with previous findings; Maynard and Dando, 1974).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on data shown in Figure 3A and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Branch order distributions varied across GM neurons, as did axonal branch point orders.
source: Branch order distributions varied across neurons, as did axonal branch point orders (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Variable axon numbers, locations, and branching patterns suggest that each GM neuron differentially integrates voltage signals arising from varying proportions of lower and higher branch orders.
source: Taken together, variable axon numbers, locations, and branching patterns suggest that each GM neuron differentially integrates voltage signals arising from varying proportions of lower and higher branch orders.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the morphological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Focal glutamate photo-uncaging evoked hyperpolarizing voltage deflections across the GM neuronal structure.
source: Focal glutamate photo-uncaging evoked hyperpolarizing voltage deflections across the neuronal structure (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The inhibitory potentials evoked by focal glutamate photo-uncaging are consistent with ionotropic glutamate-gated inhibitory currents described in previous work.
source: These inhibitory potentials are consistent with ionotropic glutamate-gated inhibitory currents described in previous work (Marder and Paupardin-Tritsch, 1978; Eisen and Marder, 1982; Marder and Eisen, 1984; Cleland and Selverston, 1995).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Voltage response amplitudes to focal glutamate photo-uncaging varied across the GM neuronal structure.
source: Although voltage responses were uniformly inhibitory across the neuronal structure, their amplitudes varied (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Focal glutamate responses were relatively stable, desensitizing only when the inter-pulse period was less than 10 s.
source: These focal glutamate responses were relatively stable, desensitizing only when the inter-pulse period (IPPs) was less than 10 s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: A non-zero response to glutamate applied to the soma was observed in only one GM neuron out of 10.
source: Across GM neurons (N = 10), a non-zero response (measured at the soma) to glutamate applied to the soma was observed in only one GM neuron.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data.

claim: The mean maximum amplitude of glutamate responses across GM neurons was 2.15 ± 1 mV.
source: Response amplitudes varied across positions with a mean maximum amplitude of 2.15 ± 1 mV.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data.

claim: The mean coefficient of variation of non-zero glutamate responses across GM neurons was 0.4 ± 0.1.
source: The mean coefficient of variation of non-zero responses, across preparations, was 0.4 ± 0.1 (N = 10), suggesting that, on average, non-zero responses varied by approximately 40% of the mean response amplitude within each neuron.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data.

claim: The electrotonic decrement of a voltage signal is dependent on the diameter of the neurite, the membrane resistance, the extent of branching, and the absolute distance the signal travels.
source: The electrotonic decrement of a voltage signal, from photo-stimulation site to recording site, is dependent on a number of factors: the diameter of the neurite through which it propagates (which influences the axial resistance to current flow), the membrane resistance, the extent of branching and associated loss of conductance at branch points, and the absolute distance the signal travels (Rall, 1959; Goldstein and Rall, 1974).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to foundational work on cable theory.

claim: Linear regression analyses of response amplitudes as a function of distance, branch order, and neurite diameter showed no significant linear relationships.
source: Linear regression analyses of response amplitudes as a function of each of these geometric parameters showed no significant linear relationships, with insignificant p-values>0.1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on statistical analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: There is no apparent dependence of somatic response amplitude on where the responses were evoked.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that there is no apparent dependence of somatic response amplitude on where the responses were evoked.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is a summary of the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: A neuron's distributed cable properties can be quantitatively assessed by measuring the reversal potentials of local glutamate responses evoked at sites varying in distance from the somatic recording site.
source: A neuron's distributed cable properties, or electrotonic structure, can be quantitatively assessed by measuring the reversal potentials (more specifically, the apparent Erevs measured at the soma) of local glutamate responses evoked at sites varying in distance from the somatic recording site (Calvin, 1969; Carnevale and Johnston, 1982).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The apparent reversal potential of an inhibitory event is independent of its maximal conductance.
source: First, we demonstrate that the apparent Erev of an inhibitory event evoked 200 µm away from the recording site (as shown in Figure 6A) is independent of its maximal conductance (or receptor density; Figure 6B–C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 6B–C.

claim: The apparent reversal potential is independent of maximal conductance magnitude, regardless of the activation site's distance from the recording site.
source: The apparent Erev is independent of gmax magnitude, regardless of the activation site's distance from the recording site (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The apparent reversal potential for a locally activated inhibitory current changes as a function of distance from the recording site.
source: Second, we show that the apparent Erev for a locally activated inhibitory current changes as a function of distance from the recording site (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: The apparent reversal potential of a locally-activated inhibitory current is independent of its maximal conductance and is dependent on the site's distance from the recording site.
source: Thus, from considering one cable model with one set of passive properties, we can deduce that the apparent Erev of a locally-activated inhibitory current is independent of its maximal conductance (or receptor density) and is dependent on the site's distance from the recording site.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is a summary of the simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The dependence of the apparent reversal potential on distance is contingent upon the effective electrotonic structure of the voltage signal's path of propagation.
source: Figure 7 demonstrates that the dependence of the apparent Erev on distance is contingent upon the effective electrotonic structure of the voltage signal's path of propagation, from activation site to recording site.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: The apparent reversal potential undergoes a greater hyperpolarizing shift with distance with decreasing electrotonic length constant values.
source: It is evident that the apparent Erev undergoes a greater hyperpolarizing shift with distance with decreasing λ values.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: As the electrotonic length constant increases, apparent reversal potentials of responses evoked at different activation site distances converge toward the actual reversal potential.
source: Considering a subset of these cable models, with λ values between 300–1700 µm, the apparent Erevs measured at different activation site distances diverge as λ decreases to 300 µm and converge as λ increases beyond 1000 µm (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Invariant apparent reversal potentials suggest a relatively high electrotonic length constant.
source: Invariant apparent Erevs suggest a relatively high electrotonic length constant, whereas heterogeneous Erevs suggest a lower electrotonic length constant.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The approach to characterizing electrotonic structure using reversal potential measurements is independent of differential maximal conductance values or receptor densities across the neuronal structure.
source: As is shown in Figure 6, this approach to characterizing the electrotonic structure, or passive cable properties, of a neuron is independent of differential gmax values, or receptor densities, across the neuronal structure.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The within-neuron coefficient of variation of apparent reversal potentials across photo-uncaging sites in GM neurons was 0.04 ± 0.01.
source: The linear fits for each position show little variation in the reversal potential across all positions within each preparation, with a within-neuron coefficient of variation of 0.04 ± 0.01 (mean ± SD; Figure 8D; Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mean reversal potentials across GM neurons varied, with a pooled mean of –78.6 ± 7 mV.
source: Although apparent Erevs were nearly invariant within each neuron, mean reversal potentials across neurons did vary, with a pooled mean of –78.6 ± 7 mV (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: Variable response amplitudes across positions yielded variable linear fit slopes within GM neurons.
source: A consequence of variable response amplitudes across positions yielded variable linear fit slopes within neurons (as shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on experimental data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Variable linear fit slopes are likely a reflection of variable receptor densities or maximal conductances at the different photo-uncaging sites.
source: This is likely a reflection of variable receptor densities or maximal conductances at the different photo-uncaging sites (consistent with the simulations shown in Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data and simulations.

claim: There was no significant linear relationship between input resistances measured at the soma and the mean within-neuron reversal potentials.
source: There was no significant linear relationship between input resistances measured at the soma (Table 2) and the mean within-neuron reversal potentials (p=0.2; data not shown graphically, but available in Table 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Linear regression analyses of apparent reversal potentials as a function of distance, branch order, and neurite diameter revealed near-zero slopes for all 10 GM neurons.
source: Lolliplots for each preparation, showing apparent Erevs for each photo-uncaging site as a function of their distance from the somatic recording site, diameter, and branch order (Figure 9), confirm no dependence of the apparent Erev on these cable properties. Linear regression analyses revealed near-zero slopes for all 10 neurons (Figure 9—figure supplement 1; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is based on statistical analyses shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: Sites varying in absolute distance, diameter, and branch order do not vary substantially in their electrotonic distance from the somatic recording site in GM neurons.
source: This suggests that, even though these sites vary in their absolute distance, diameter, and branch order, they do not vary substantially in their electrotonic distance from the somatic recording site.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The minimal hyperpolarizing shift for apparent reversal potentials measured for activation sites between 100 and 800 µm from the recording site is consistent with an electrotonic length constant greater than 1.5 mm.
source: The minimal hyperpolarizing shift for apparent Erevs measured for activation sites between 100 and 800 µm from the recording site is consistent with a λ > 1.5 mm (referencing Figure 7D and E).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is inferred by comparing experimental data to simulations shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: GM neurons are surprisingly electrotonically compact, despite their expansive structures and morphological complexity.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that GM neurons are surprisingly electrotonically compact, despite their expansive structures and morphological complexity.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Despite their expansive and complex morphologies, GM neurons have electrotonically compact structures.
source: Here, we present the ostensible conundrum wherein an identifiable neuron type, despite its complex, highly-branched, neurite tree, is surprisingly electrotonically compact.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is a summary of the main finding.

claim: This result differs from studies in a variety of neuron types that attribute specific physiological computations and plasticity rules to compartmentalized electrotonic structures.
source: This result differs from studies in a variety of neuron types that attribute specific physiological computations and plasticity rules to compartmentalized electrotonic structures.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Structural complexity does not necessarily yield compartmentalized computations.
source: The present work differs from these other studies of neuronal electrotonus and enriches our framework for understanding how morphology maps (or does not map) to physiological function. Otherwise stated: structural complexity does not necessarily yield compartmentalized computations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In GM neurons, synaptic voltage events may propagate tortuous neurite paths that extend beyond half a millimeter in length.
source: In GM neurons, synaptic voltage events may propagate tortuous neurite paths that extend beyond half a millimeter in length (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on morphological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Current can be injected at the somatic recording site and effectively alter the membrane potential at distal sites in GM neurons.
source: Yet, current can be injected at the somatic recording site and effectively alter the membrane potential at such distal and distant sites allowing for reasonable apparent Erevs (approximately −80 mV).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on experimental data.

claim: The amplitude of the voltage response at the photo-uncaging site must be larger than what is observed at the soma.
source: Likewise, the amplitude of the voltage response at the photo-uncaging site must be larger than what we observe at the soma.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The electrotonic decrement of distal events initiated as far as 1 mm away must be small enough so that apparent reversal potentials can be recorded at the soma.
source: Because distally evoked events, initiated as far as 1 mm away, can be observed at the somatic recording site, the electrotonic decrement of these distal events must be small enough so that apparent reversal potentials can be recorded.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The invariance in apparent reversal potentials across sites suggests relatively little variance in the electrotonic decrement of signals coming from disparate sites across the neurite tree.
source: Lastly, the invariance in apparent Erevs across sites (a measure independent of receptor density) suggests relatively little variance in the electrotonic decrement of signals coming from disparate sites across the neurite tree.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: GM neurons function almost like a single compartment, despite their complex structures.
source: In this sense, these neurons function almost like a single compartment, despite their complex structures.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The geometric and/or passive cable properties provide the most plausible explanation for the electrotonically compact structure of GM neurons.
source: The geometric and/or passive cable properties provide the most plausible explanation for this electrotonically compact structure.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The primary neurite of GM neurons can be as large as 15–20 µm in diameter.
source: Recent work has quantified the fine anatomical properties of GM neurons and other STG neuron types, showing that the primary neurite can be as large as 15–20 µm in diameter and that the most distal neurite branches may taper to diameters between <1 and 10 µm (Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The most distal neurite branches of GM neurons may taper to diameters between <1 and 10 µm.
source: Recent work has quantified the fine anatomical properties of GM neurons and other STG neuron types, showing that the primary neurite can be as large as 15–20 µm in diameter and that the most distal neurite branches may taper to diameters between <1 and 10 µm (Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: GM neurites may have relatively low axial resistances as a consequence of large neurite diameters.
source: GM neurites may have relatively low axial resistances as a consequence of large neurite diameters.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the morphological data.

claim: Voltage signal decrement may be minimized by high membrane resistances across neurite branches in GM neurons.
source: It is possible that voltage signal decrement may also be minimized by high membrane resistances across neurite branches.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is speculative.

claim: The input resistance as measured at the soma is likely a reflection of the resistance of the membrane surface area of much of the entire neuron in electrotonically compact neurons.
source: Given that these neurons are electrotonically compact, the input resistance as measured at the soma is likely a reflection of the resistance of the membrane surface area of much of the entire neuron.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the electrotonic compactness.

claim: Input resistances measured at the soma in GM neurons are relatively low (mean of approximately 10 MΩ).
source: Thus, it is not surprising that input resistances measured at the soma are relatively low (mean of approximately 10 MΩ (Table 2), consistent with many years of recordings from STG neurons).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: If the neuron were less electrotonically compact, the input resistance measured at the soma would be higher.
source: If the neuron were less electrotonically compact, the input resistance measured at the soma would be higher, as the measurement would be restricted to the surface area of the local, somatic membrane.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from cable theory principles.

claim: Some neuron types compensate for passive attenuation of voltage responses with distance-dependent scaling of synaptic receptor density.
source: Other neuron types compensate for passive attenuation of voltage responses with distance-dependent scaling of synaptic receptor density (Andrasfalvy and Magee, 2001; Magee and Cook, 2000; Smith et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Variable response amplitudes in GM neurons likely arise from local variations in receptor densities.
source: Due to the uniformity of their apparent Erevs, it is likely that these variable response amplitudes arise from local variations in receptor densities.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: It is unlikely that receptor densities in GM neurons are scaling with distance in a systematic way.
source: Because the response amplitudes across sites vary in a manner that is independent of distance from the recording site (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table 1), it is unlikely that receptor densities are scaling with distance in a systematic way.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The experiments provide an 'upper bound' on the effective electrotonic length constant and compactness of GM neurons.
source: These experiments provide an 'upper bound' on the effective electrotonic length constant and, therefore, the compactness of GM neurons.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental conditions.

claim: The experiments were done in TTX, wherein TTX-sensitive, voltage-gated sodium channels are blocked and circuit activity is silenced.
source: These experiments were done in TTX, wherein TTX-sensitive, voltage-gated sodium channels are blocked and circuit activity is silenced.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and describes the experimental conditions.

claim: No change in input resistance as measured at the soma was detected before and after TTX addition.
source: While the overall membrane conductance may be higher in the absence of TTX (although, no change in input resistance as measured at the soma was detected before and after TTX addition), we would not expect these TTX-sensitive currents to substantially alter inhibitory voltage signal propagation at the range of membrane potentials probed here (−120 to −40 mV).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is based on experimental observations.

claim: It is unlikely that TTX-sensitive voltage-gated channels would shunt the current arising from evoked events in GM neurons.
source: Furthermore, spike initiation zones, where TTX-sensitive channels are most likely to reside, are located in the periphery, where the axons exit the neuropil (Raper, 1979; Miller, 1980). Thus, it is unlikely that TTX-sensitive voltage-gated channels would shunt the current arising from these evoked events in the same way as has been seen in other systems (Laurent, 1990).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the location of spike initiation zones and supported by citations.

claim: Separation of synaptic integration and slow waves from spike initiation zones may be a morphological strategy to avoid shunting of synaptic currents in STG neurons.
source: In STG neurons, it is an intriguing possibility that separation of synaptic integration and slow waves from spike initiation zones may be a morphological strategy established to avoid shunting of synaptic currents.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is speculative.

claim: The identified neurons of the STG exhibit complex morphologies.
source: The identified neurons of the STG exhibit complex morphologies (Wilensky et al., 2003; Baldwin and Graubard, 1995; Bucher et al., 2007; Goeritz et al., 2013; Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All STG neurons display large somata (50–150 µm in diameter) and primary neurites that ramify throughout the STG neuropil.
source: Like the GM neuron, all STG neurons display large somata (50–150 µm in diameter) and primary neurites that ramify throughout the STG neuropil, wherein synaptic partners form numerous, sparse synapses (King, 1976a, 1976b; Baldwin and Graubard, 1995).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: If each STG neuron type were highly electrotonically compartmentalized, yet variable across animals, wiring this circuit would be a puzzling developmental task.
source: If each neuron type were highly electrotonically compartmentalized, yet variable across animals, wiring this circuit would be a puzzling developmental task.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is speculative.

claim: The fact that STG neurons present electrotonically compact structures simplifies understanding of the developmental wiring rules that may be required.
source: The fact that these neurons present electrotonically compact structures simplifies our understanding of the developmental wiring rules that may be required and how such a circuit can be relatively immune to structural differences.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The neurons of the STG rely on graded transmission and slow oscillations, rather than fast spikes, to maintain phase relationships at the circuit level.
source: The neurons of the STG rely on graded transmission and slow oscillations, rather than fast spikes, to maintain phase relationships at the circuit level (Graubard, 1978; Raper, 1979; Graubard et al., 1980, 1983; Anderson and Barker, 1981; Manor et al., 1997, 1999; Bose et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An electrotonically compact structure is sufficient for integrating activity of many, yet sparsely distributed, synaptic inputs from each presynaptic neuron, independent of synaptic site locations.
source: Given the relatively slow temporal precision of this circuit, an electrotonically compact structure is sufficient for integrating activity of many, yet sparsely distributed, synaptic inputs from each presynaptic neuron (King, 1976a, 1976b), independent of synaptic site locations.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: Electrotonic compactness both masks the observed heterogeneity in glutamate sensitivity across the neuronal structure and diminishes the consequences of presumed variability in synaptic site location.
source: In this way, electrotonic compactness both masks the observed heterogeneity in glutamate sensitivity across the neuronal structure (Figures 4 and 5) and diminishes the consequences of presumed variability in synaptic site location arising from observed animal-to-animal variability in GM morphology (also see Otopalik et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Presynaptic inputs may influence GM neuron activity with equivalent efficacy regardless of synaptic site location.
source: In this scenario, presynaptic inputs may influence GM neuron activity with equivalent efficacy regardless of synaptic site location.
evidence: The claim is stated in the Discussion section and is inferred from the electrotonic compactness.

claim: Synaptic democracy is achieved by combining an electrotonically compact structure with graded transmission resilient to electrotonic decrement across sparsely distributed, synchronous presynaptic sites.
source: This synaptic democracy (Häusser, 2001) is achieved by combining an electrotonically compact structure with graded transmission resilient to electrotonic decrement across sparsely distributed, synchronous presynaptic sites.
